key_terms.meaning: A finite formula built from ∅, ε and alphabet symbols using union, concatenation and Kleene star; it denotes a language.
Kleene star binds tightest, then concatenation, then union: a ∪ bc* means a ∪ (b·(c*)).
R* = {ε} ∪ R ∪ RR ∪ RRR ∪ …, all finite concatenations of strings from R.
The expression ε denotes the language {ε}, a language with one string of length zero; it is not the empty language.
The expression ∅ denotes the language with no strings at all; ∅* = {ε} but ∅·R = ∅.
Identities such as R ∪ ∅ = R, Rε = R, (R*)* = R*, R(S ∪ T) = RS ∪ RT that allow rewriting without automata.
A recursive build that turns each RE operator into a small ε-NFA fragment with one start and one final state.
ε-closure(q) is the set of states reachable from q by following zero or more ε-moves only.
Repeatedly remove a DFA state and label the remaining edges with regular expressions so the last edge carries the answer.
If X = A X ∪ B and A does not contain ε, then X = A*B is the unique solution; used to solve state equations.
A language is regular if and only if it is denoted by some regular expression; FA and RE have equal power.
Every regular language L has a length p such that any w in L with |w| ≥ p splits as xyz with |xy| ≤ p, |y| ≥ 1 and xyⁱz in L for all i ≥ 0.
The constant in the pumping lemma, at most the number of states of a DFA that accepts the language.
A class is closed under an operation if applying it to members always gives a member; regular languages are closed under union, intersection, complement, concatenation and star.
A yes/no question about a language that an algorithm can always answer, such as emptiness, finiteness or equality of two regular languages.
x ≡_L y means for every suffix z, xz is in L exactly when yz is in L; the classes partition Σ*.
Strings x and y are distinguishable by L if some suffix z puts exactly one of xz, yz inside L.
The number of equivalence classes of the Myhill–Nerode relation; finite index means L is regular, and the index equals the states of the minimal DFA.
The unique (up to renaming) DFA with the fewest states for a regular language, obtained by merging indistinguishable states.
A finite automaton has no unbounded counter or stack, so it cannot match balanced brackets or compare two counts that grow without limit.

takeaways: A regular expression is just a finite formula, so it can only describe patterns that need a fixed, finite amount of memory to check.
Precedence matters: star first, then concatenation, then union, and parentheses override everything.
The algebraic laws let you simplify an expression or prove two expressions equal without drawing a single state.
Thompson's construction builds an ε-NFA operator by operator, so the machine is correct by construction rather than by insight.
Arden's theorem turns state equations into a tidy closed-form expression and is the quickest hand method for DFA to RE.
Kleene's theorem is the bridge of the whole unit: DFA, NFA, ε-NFA and regular expressions all describe the same languages.
The pumping lemma is a one-way test: failing it proves a language is not regular, passing it proves nothing.
Myhill–Nerode is exact in both directions and also gives the smallest DFA, which the pumping lemma cannot do.
Closure and decision properties mean you can answer many questions about regular languages by pure machine manipulation, with no cleverness required.
Regular expressions power search boxes, tokenizers and network filters, but nested structure needs a pushdown automaton instead.
bank_note: Long answers usually ask for a full construction with a diagram plus a proof of correctness, and for pumping-lemma proofs examiners insist on the pumping length, the split, and the choice of the index i that breaks the language.

bank.q: Define a regular expression over an alphabet Σ. List the operators with their precedence and give regular expressions for: strings over {a,b} ending in bb, strings with an even number of a's, and strings containing exactly one b.
outline: Recursive definition: ∅, ε and each a in Σ are REs; if R and S are REs then R ∪ S, RS and R* are REs
Precedence: star > concatenation > union, with parentheses to override
(a ∪ b)*bb for ending in bb
(b ∪ ab*a)* for even number of a's, or equivalent
a*ba* for exactly one b
Note that ε and ∅ are different expressions with different languages

bank.q: State Kleene's theorem and explain both directions of the proof in outline, saying which construction handles which direction.
outline: Statement: L is regular iff L = L(R) for some regular expression R
RE to FA: Thompson's construction builds an ε-NFA for each operator, inductively on the expression
FA to RE: state elimination or Arden's theorem on state equations
Conclusion: the three models define exactly the same class, the regular languages
Mention that the constructions are effective, so they give algorithms, not just existence

bank.q: State the pumping lemma for regular languages and explain the intuition behind each of its three conditions.
outline: Full statement with the quantifiers: there exists p, for all w with |w| ≥ p, there exist x, y, z
|xy| ≤ p: the cycle is reached within the first p symbols
|y| ≥ 1: the loop is a real loop, so y is non-empty
xyⁱz in L for all i ≥ 0: looping i times, including zero times, stays in L
Pigeonhole argument on the sequence of p+1 states visited while reading w

bank.q: List the closure properties of regular languages and, for any three of them, describe the construction that proves the property.
outline: Closure under union, intersection, complement, concatenation, Kleene star, reversal, difference, homomorphism
Union and concatenation via ε-NFA with a new start state
Intersection and difference via the product construction on two DFAs
Complement by swapping final and non-final states of a complete DFA
State that closure under intersection follows from De Morgan's laws plus union and complement

bank.q: State the Myhill–Nerode theorem and explain how the index of the relation is related to the number of states of the minimal DFA.
outline: Definition of x ≡_L y: for every z, xz in L iff yz in L
≡_L is an equivalence relation: reflexive, symmetric, transitive
Theorem: L is regular iff ≡_L has finitely many classes
The classes are exactly the states of the minimal DFA, so index = minimum state count
Right-invariance: if x ≡_L y then xa ≡_L ya for every symbol a

bank.q: Convert the regular expression (a ∪ b)*abb into an ε-NFA using Thompson's construction. Show each intermediate fragment and mark the ε-moves.
outline: Basic fragments for a, b, and the union fragment with a new start and a new final state joined by ε-moves
Star fragment: new start and final state, ε from new start to old start and old final, ε back from old final to old start
Concatenation by merging the final state of one fragment with the start of the next using ε
Final ε-NFA with one start state and one final state
Correctness statement: the fragment for R accepts exactly L(R)

bank.q: Write the state equations for a given two- or three-state DFA and solve them using Arden's theorem to obtain the equivalent regular expression.
outline: Name each state's language variable, e.g. X₀, X₁, X₂
Write one equation per state: Xᵢ = a Xⱼ ∪ b Xₖ ∪ (ε if Xᵢ is final)
Solve from the last state backwards, or substitute to get the form X = A X ∪ B
Apply Arden: X = A*B, valid only when ε is not in A
Substitute back and simplify with the algebraic laws to get the expression for the start state

bank.q: Use the pumping lemma to prove that L = {aⁿbⁿ : n ≥ 0} is not regular. Write every step with the quantifiers in the correct order.
outline: Assume L is regular, so it has pumping length p
Choose w = aᵖbᵖ, which is in L and has length 2p ≥ p
By the lemma w = xyz with |xy| ≤ p and |y| ≥ 1, so y = aᵏ for some k ≥ 1
Pump with i = 0: xy⁰z = aᵖ⁻ᵏbᵖ has unequal counts, so it is not in L
Contradiction, hence L is not regular
Remark that choosing w to force y inside the a-block is the key step

bank.q: Given a DFA, minimise it by the table-filling (or partition refinement) method and justify each merge using indistinguishability of states.
outline: Remove unreachable states, then separate final from non-final states
Mark pairs distinguishable if one is final and the other is not
Propagate: mark (p,q) if for some symbol a the pair (δ(p,a), δ(q,a)) is marked
Repeat until no new pairs are marked; unmarked pairs are equivalent
Build the quotient automaton from the equivalence classes and state why it is minimal

bank.q: Describe decision procedures, using finite automata, for these questions about regular languages: emptiness, finiteness, membership of a string, and equality of two languages.
outline: Emptiness: check for a path from start to a final state by reachability
Finiteness: the language is infinite iff a cycle is reachable from the start and can reach a final state
Membership: run the DFA on the string, accept if it ends in a final state
Equality of L₁ and L₂: build the product DFA and test whether the symmetric difference is empty
All procedures terminate because the automata are finite

bank.q: Explain, with a small example, how a lexical analyser uses regular expressions and finite automata to tokenise a program, and where the technique stops working.
outline: Each token class (identifier, integer, keyword, operator) is written as a regular expression
The expressions are converted to one combined NFA, then to a DFA, then to a table-driven program
Longest-match and rule-order conventions resolve conflicts
Limitation: nested comments, balanced brackets and block structure are not regular
Those parts are handed to a parser built from a context-free grammar

bank.q: 'The pumping lemma can prove a language non-regular but never regular.' Discuss this statement, and explain why Myhill–Nerode does not have the same weakness.
outline: Pumping lemma is a necessary condition only, so satisfying it proves nothing
Sketch of a non-regular language that still satisfies the pumping conditions
Myhill–Nerode is an if-and-only-if: finitely many classes iff regular
Failing the pumping lemma means non-regular; a finite index in Myhill–Nerode means regular
Practical advice: use pumping for quick disproofs, Myhill–Nerode when a proof of regularity or a minimal DFA is needed

bank.q: Compare the state elimination method and Arden's theorem for converting a DFA to a regular expression. Which would you use for a small automaton by hand, and what happens to the size of the expression as the automaton grows?
outline: State elimination: delete states one by one, updating edge labels with unions and stars
Arden: write and solve linear equations over languages
Arden needs the ε-free condition on the coefficient language; state elimination does not
Both give correct but possibly long expressions; expressions can grow exponentially in the number of states
For hand work on two to four states, Arden is usually shorter; elimination is easier to present as an algorithm

bank.q: 'Finite automata cannot count.' Explain precisely what this means, use it to show that balanced parentheses and {aⁿbⁿcⁿ : n ≥ 0} are not regular, and state which machine class can handle them.
outline: A DFA has a fixed finite number of states, so memory is bounded and independent of the input
Any unbounded count would need infinitely many states
Balanced brackets require matching an unbounded number of opens with closes
Intersection argument or pumping lemma for aⁿbⁿcⁿ
A pushdown automaton with a stack recognises both, giving context-free languages
Note the hierarchy: regular ⊂ context-free ⊂ recursive

bank.q: Prove that regular languages are closed under complement and intersection, and use these results to show closure under difference. Then explain why the intersection proof does not carry over directly for non-deterministic automata.
outline: Complement: complete the DFA, then swap final and non-final states
Intersection: product construction, final states are pairs where both components are final
Difference: L₁ ∩ complement(L₂)
Determinism is needed for complement, since swapping states of an NFA does not complement its language
Simultaneous simulation on all NFA states fixes the problem, at a cost in state count

glossary.def: A finite, non-empty set of symbols, for example Σ = {0,1}.
A finite sequence of symbols drawn from an alphabet; ε is the string of length zero.
A set of strings over a fixed alphabet, possibly infinite, possibly empty.
A finite formula built from ∅, ε and alphabet symbols using union, concatenation and Kleene star.
R* is the set of all strings made by concatenating zero or more strings from R.
R ∪ S denotes the set of strings that are in R or in S, written with a plus sign in some books.
RS is the set of strings xy where x comes from R and y comes from S.
A non-deterministic finite automaton whose transitions may be taken without reading any symbol.
The set of states reachable from a state using only ε-moves, including the state itself.
An inductive procedure that builds an ε-NFA fragment for every operator of a regular expression.
A DFA-to-RE method that removes states one by one while relabelling the remaining edges with regular expressions.
If X = A X ∪ B and ε is not in A, then X = A*B is the only solution for X.
The statement that finite automata and regular expressions accept exactly the same languages.
A necessary condition that every regular language must satisfy, used to prove non-regularity.
The constant p in the pumping lemma, bounded by the number of states of an accepting DFA.
The guarantee that applying an operation to languages of a class always yields a language of the same class.
An always-terminating algorithm that answers a yes/no question about a language.
Building a machine whose states are pairs of states of two given machines, used for intersection and union.
x ≡_L y holds when every suffix z keeps xz and yz on the same side of L.
Two strings are distinguishable by L if some suffix places exactly one of them in L.
The number of equivalence classes of a relation; for ≡_L the index is the size of the minimal DFA.
The smallest DFA for a regular language, unique up to renaming of states.
The set of strings over the alphabet that are not in the language, written L̄ or Σ* − L.
A language accepted by a pushdown automaton, which can handle unbounded nesting that regular languages cannot.
